PA.name: Pennsylvania
state_specific_notes: Pennsylvania is a two-party consent state for audio recordings (18 Pa.C.S. Section 5703). Recording police in public is generally protected, but be aware of wiretapping laws for audio.
Pennsylvania has a 'stop and identify' culture but no statute requiring you to provide ID during a pedestrian stop unless you are driving.
Under PA law, police must have probable cause or a warrant to search your vehicle unless you consent.
Philadelphia has specific policies on police conduct through its Police Advisory Commission.

rights.description: You are required to provide your license, registration, and insurance. Beyond that, you have the right to remain silent under the 5th Amendment. You may say: 'I am exercising my right to remain silent.'
rights.source: 5th Amendment, U.S. Constitution; Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966)

rights.description: You do not have to consent to a search of your vehicle. Officers need probable cause or a warrant. Clearly state: 'I do not consent to a search.'
rights.source: 4th Amendment, U.S. Constitution; Schneckloth v. Bustamonte, 412 U.S. 218 (1973)

rights.description: You may record police during a traffic stop. However, PA is a two-party consent state for audio, so be aware. Visual recording in public is generally protected under the 1st Amendment.
rights.source: Glik v. Cunniffe, 655 F.3d 78 (1st Cir. 2011); 18 Pa.C.S. Section 5703

rights.right: Right to Know the Reason for the Stop
rights.description: You have the right to ask why you were stopped. Officers must have reasonable suspicion of a traffic violation or crime.
If you are arrested, you have the right to an attorney. If you cannot afford one, one will be appointed. Invoke this right clearly.
rights.source: 6th Amendment, U.S. Constitution; Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963)

de_escalation_tips: Keep your hands on the steering wheel where the officer can see them.
Turn on your interior light if it is dark outside.
Inform the officer before reaching for your license or registration.
Do not argue about the reason for the stop -- contest it in court instead.
If you receive a citation, sign it. Signing is not an admission of guilt.

rights.right: Right to Ask if You Are Being Detained
rights.description: You may ask: 'Am I being detained or am I free to go?' If you are not being detained, you may calmly walk away.
rights.source: Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968); Florida v. Bostick, 501 U.S. 429 (1991)

rights.description: You are not required to answer questions. You may state: 'I am exercising my right to remain silent.'
You do not have to consent to a pat-down or search unless the officer has reasonable suspicion you are armed and dangerous.
rights.source: 4th Amendment, U.S. Constitution; Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968)

rights.description: Pennsylvania does not have a stop-and-identify statute. You are generally not required to show ID during a pedestrian stop unless you are operating a vehicle.
rights.source: Hiibel v. Sixth Judicial District, 542 U.S. 177 (2004) (PA has no such statute)

rights.description: You have the right to record police activity in public spaces. Do not interfere with their duties while recording.

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and keep your hands visible.
Do not run or make sudden movements.
Politely ask if you are being detained.
If detained, invoke your right to remain silent.
Remember officer details (badge number, name, patrol car number) for later.

rights.right: Right to Refuse Entry Without a Warrant
rights.description: Police cannot enter your home without a valid warrant, your consent, or exigent circumstances. Ask to see the warrant before opening the door.
rights.source: 4th Amendment, U.S. Constitution; Payton v. New York, 445 U.S. 573 (1980)

rights.description: A valid search warrant must be signed by a judge, list your specific address, and describe what is to be searched. You may ask to read it.
You do not have to answer questions at your door. You may speak through a closed door.
You may request to have an attorney present before answering any questions or allowing a search.
If officers have a valid warrant and enter your home, you have the right to observe the search and note what is taken.

de_escalation_tips: Speak through a closed door if possible.
Ask to see a warrant before opening the door.
If you choose to speak, step outside and close the door behind you.
Do not physically block officers who have a valid warrant.
Document everything they take and ask for a receipt of seized items.

rights.description: The 1st Amendment protects your right to peacefully assemble and protest in public spaces. Permits may be required for large gatherings.
rights.source: 1st Amendment, U.S. Constitution; Cox v. Louisiana, 379 U.S. 536 (1965)

rights.description: You may photograph and record police and public events in public spaces. Officers cannot order you to stop recording or seize your device without a warrant.
rights.source: 1st Amendment; Glik v. Cunniffe, 655 F.3d 78 (1st Cir. 2011)

rights.description: Before arresting protesters, police must generally issue a clear dispersal order and give reasonable time to comply.

rights.right: Right to Remain Silent if Detained
rights.description: If detained or arrested during a protest, you have the right to remain silent and request an attorney.
If injured during a protest or while in custody, you have the right to receive medical attention.
rights.source: 8th Amendment, U.S. Constitution; Estelle v. Gamble, 429 U.S. 97 (1976)

de_escalation_tips: Stay with a group and avoid isolated areas.
Follow lawful dispersal orders to avoid arrest.
Keep your hands visible and avoid throwing objects.
Have a legal observer or buddy system in place.
Write an emergency legal contact number on your arm in permanent marker.

rights.right: Right to Remain Silent About Immigration Status
rights.description: You do not have to answer questions about where you were born, your immigration status, or how you entered the US. This applies to everyone regardless of status.

rights.right: Right to Refuse Consent to Search
rights.description: You do not have to consent to a search of yourself, your belongings, or your home. Clearly state that you do not consent.
You have the right to speak with an attorney before answering questions or signing any documents. Do not sign voluntary departure forms without legal counsel.

rights.right: Right to a Hearing Before an Immigration Judge
rights.description: In most cases, you have the right to appear before an immigration judge and present your case before being removed from the country.
rights.source: INA Section 240; Zadvydas v. Davis, 533 U.S. 678 (2001)

rights.description: Foreign nationals have the right to contact their country's consulate if detained. Law enforcement is required to inform you of this right.
rights.source: Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, Article 36

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and do not run.
State clearly: 'I am exercising my right to remain silent.'
Do not provide false documents or information.
Do not sign any documents without speaking to an attorney.
Memorize the phone number of an immigration attorney or hotline.

rights.description: The 5th Amendment protects you from being compelled to be a witness against yourself. You may decline to answer questions from law enforcement.
rights.source: 5th Amendment, U.S. Constitution; Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966)

rights.right: Right Against Unreasonable Search and Seizure
rights.description: The 4th Amendment protects you from unreasonable searches. Officers need a warrant, probable cause, or your consent to search.
rights.source: 4th Amendment, U.S. Constitution; Mapp v. Ohio, 367 U.S. 643 (1961)

rights.description: You have the right to an attorney during custodial interrogation and at trial. If you cannot afford one, one will be appointed.
You generally have the right to record police officers performing their duties in public. Do not interfere with their work.

rights.right: Right to Know if You Are Being Detained
rights.description: You may ask an officer: 'Am I being detained or am I free to go?' This clarifies your legal status in the encounter.

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and breathe steadily.
Keep your hands visible at all times.
Be polite and do not argue.
Invoke your rights clearly and calmly.
Document the encounter afterward: write down times, badge numbers, and details.

CA.name: California
state_specific_notes: California is a two-party consent state for confidential communications (CA Penal Code Section 632). However, recording police in public is protected.
California has the TRUST Act (AB 4) and California Values Act (SB 54) which limit state/local law enforcement cooperation with federal immigration authorities.
Under Proposition 64, marijuana possession for adults 21+ is legal, but driving under the influence remains illegal.
California requires officers to provide their name and badge number upon request (CA Penal Code Section 830.10).
Los Angeles, San Francisco, and other cities have sanctuary city policies providing additional protections.

rights.description: You must provide license, registration, and insurance. Beyond that, you may remain silent. Say: 'I am invoking my 5th Amendment right to remain silent.'
rights.source: 5th Amendment; CA Constitution Art. I, Section 15

rights.description: You do not have to consent to a vehicle search. California requires probable cause or a warrant. Say: 'I do not consent to a search.'
You may record your traffic stop. In California, recording police performing public duties is protected. Passengers may also record.
rights.source: 1st Amendment; CA Penal Code Section 69 (does not apply to recording)

rights.right: Right to Refuse Field Sobriety Tests (Pre-Arrest)
rights.description: You may refuse voluntary field sobriety tests before arrest without penalty. However, refusing a chemical test after arrest can result in license suspension under implied consent law.
California officers must provide their name and badge number when requested.

de_escalation_tips: Pull over in a safe, well-lit area as soon as practical.
Turn off your engine and turn on interior lights at night.
Keep hands on the steering wheel until asked for documents.
Narrate your actions: 'I am reaching for my glove box now.'
If cited, sign the ticket -- it is not an admission of guilt.

rights.right: Right to Ask if You Are Detained
rights.description: Ask: 'Am I being detained?' If not, you may calmly leave. Officers need reasonable suspicion to detain you.
rights.source: Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968); In re Tony C., 21 Cal.3d 888 (1978)

rights.description: You do not have to answer questions. California has no stop-and-identify statute for pedestrians.
You may refuse a search of your person or belongings unless the officer has reasonable suspicion you are armed.
You may record any interaction with police in public. Officers cannot demand you stop recording.
Under SB 54, California law enforcement cannot use resources to investigate, interrogate, detain, or arrest persons for immigration enforcement purposes.

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and keep your hands visible.
Do not run or make sudden movements.
Politely ask: 'Officer, am I free to go?'
Do not physically resist even if the stop seems unlawful.
Note the officer's badge number and patrol car number.

rights.right: Right to Refuse Entry Without a Warrant
rights.description: Do not open the door. Ask: 'Do you have a warrant?' A judicial warrant (signed by a judge) is required. An ICE administrative warrant is NOT sufficient to enter.
rights.source: 4th Amendment; Payton v. New York, 445 U.S. 573 (1980)

rights.description: Ask the officer to slide the warrant under the door. Verify it has the correct address, is signed by a judge, and is not expired.
You do not have to answer any questions through the door or otherwise.
Under SB 54, California law enforcement cannot assist federal immigration agents in enforcement actions at your home.
You have the right to speak with a lawyer before opening the door or answering questions.

de_escalation_tips: Do not open the door. Communicate through the door or a window.
Ask: 'Do you have a judicial warrant signed by a judge?'
If they have a valid warrant, do not physically resist entry.
Stay calm and state that you wish to speak with an attorney.
Ask for a list of items seized and a copy of the warrant.

rights.description: California strongly protects the right to protest. You may assemble on public sidewalks and parks without a permit for small groups.
rights.source: 1st Amendment; CA Constitution Art. I, Section 2 and 3

rights.description: You may record police and protest activity in all public spaces. Officers cannot seize your device without a warrant.
Officers must have probable cause to arrest you. Peaceful protest alone is not grounds for arrest.
Before declaring an unlawful assembly, police must issue a clear order to disperse and provide a reasonable exit route.
rights.source: CA Penal Code Section 409; CA Penal Code Section 726

rights.description: If injured during a protest or in police custody, you have the right to receive medical attention.

de_escalation_tips: Protest peacefully and do not block emergency vehicles.
Follow dispersal orders and move to the designated exit route.
Have a designated legal observer in your group.
Keep your hands visible and avoid confrontation.
Carry the phone number of a civil rights lawyer written on your body.

rights.description: You do not have to answer questions about your immigration status, country of origin, or how you entered the US.
California state and local law enforcement cannot use resources to assist federal immigration enforcement. They cannot ask about your immigration status.
You have the right to an attorney. In California, detained immigrants may qualify for free legal representation through the California SAFE program.

rights.right: Right to Refuse to Sign Documents
rights.description: Do not sign any documents, especially voluntary departure forms, without first speaking to an attorney.
If detained, you have the right to contact your country's consulate.
rights.source: Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, Article 36

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and do not flee.
Say: 'I am exercising my right to remain silent.'
Do not carry false identification documents.
Do not sign any documents without an attorney present.
Know the number of a local immigration legal aid organization.

rights.description: You have the right to decline to answer questions from law enforcement under the 5th Amendment.
Officers need a warrant, probable cause, or your consent to search you, your vehicle, or your home.
You have the right to an attorney at any critical stage of criminal proceedings.
You have the right to record police performing duties in public spaces.
California law requires officers to identify themselves with name and badge number upon request.

de_escalation_tips: Remain calm and respectful.
Keep your hands where the officer can see them.
Invoke your rights clearly and politely.
Do not physically resist.
Write down everything after the encounter.

NY.name: New York
state_specific_notes: New York is a one-party consent state for recordings (NY Penal Law Section 250.00). You may record your own conversations with police.
New York City has additional civilian oversight through the Civilian Complaint Review Board (CCRB).
The Right to Know Act requires NYPD officers to identify themselves and explain the reason for certain law enforcement activities.
New York ended cash bail for most misdemeanors and non-violent felonies.
NYC has sanctuary city policies limiting cooperation with ICE.

rights.description: Provide license, registration, and insurance when asked. You do not have to answer other questions.
You may refuse a search of your vehicle. Officers need probable cause or a warrant.
New York is a one-party consent state. You may freely record your traffic stop, including audio.

rights.right: Right to Know Why You Were Stopped
rights.description: Under the NYC Right to Know Act, officers must explain the reason for the stop.
rights.source: NYC Right to Know Act (2018); Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968)

rights.description: If arrested, you have the right to an attorney. New York has robust public defender services.

de_escalation_tips: Pull over safely and turn on your hazard lights.
Keep your hands on the steering wheel.
Inform the officer before making any movements.
Be polite; contest any disagreements in court.
If asked to exit the vehicle, comply calmly.

rights.right: Right to Ask if You Are Being Detained
rights.description: Ask: 'Am I being detained?' Under NY law, police need reasonable suspicion to stop you. If not detained, you may leave.
rights.source: Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968); People v. De Bour, 40 N.Y.2d 210 (1976)

rights.description: New York does not have a stop-and-identify statute. You are not required to show ID during a pedestrian stop.
rights.source: 5th Amendment; People v. De Bour, 40 N.Y.2d 210 (1976)

rights.description: You may refuse a frisk unless the officer reasonably believes you are armed. State: 'I do not consent to a search.'
In NYC, officers must provide a business card with their name, rank, shield number, and command under the Right to Know Act.
You may record any police interaction in public. NY is a one-party consent state.

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and keep hands visible.
Politely ask: 'Am I free to go?'
Do not run or make sudden movements.
If frisked unlawfully, do not resist -- document it afterward.
Request the officer's business card (NYC).

rights.right: Right to Refuse Entry Without a Warrant
rights.description: You do not have to open the door without a judicial warrant. An ICE administrative warrant does not authorize entry.
rights.source: 4th Amendment; Payton v. New York, 445 U.S. 573 (1980)

rights.description: Ask to see the warrant. It must be signed by a judge, list the correct address, and specify what is to be searched or who is to be arrested.
You do not have to answer questions through your door or otherwise.
Request an attorney before answering questions or allowing entry.
NYC Executive Order 41 prohibits city employees (including NYPD) from inquiring about immigration status.

de_escalation_tips: Do not open the door. Talk through the door.
Ask: 'Do you have a warrant signed by a judge?'
If they have a valid warrant, do not resist entry.
Call an attorney immediately.
Note the names and badge numbers of all officers.

rights.description: New York strongly protects the right to protest. Sidewalks and parks are traditional public forums.
rights.source: 1st Amendment; NY Constitution Art. I, Section 9

rights.description: You may record police and protest activity. NY is one-party consent for audio.
Police must give a clear and audible dispersal order before arresting protesters for unlawful assembly.
Officers may not use excessive force against protesters. The Eric Garner Anti-Chokehold Act bans chokeholds by NYPD.
If injured during a protest or in custody, you have the right to medical care.

de_escalation_tips: Protest peacefully and follow dispersal orders.
Stay with a group and have a legal observer.
Do not block traffic or emergency vehicles without a permit.
Keep hands visible and avoid confrontation.
Know the NLG legal hotline number: (212) 679-6018.

rights.description: You do not have to answer questions about immigration status, national origin, or how you entered the US.
NYPD will not ask about your immigration status or assist ICE in civil immigration enforcement under Executive Order 41.
rights.source: NYC Executive Order 41; NYC Admin Code Section 14-154

rights.description: NYC provides free legal representation to detained immigrants through the New York Immigrant Family Unity Project (NYIFUP).

rights.right: Right to Refuse to Sign Documents
rights.description: Do not sign voluntary departure or any other immigration documents without consulting an attorney.
If detained, you have the right to contact your country's consulate.
rights.source: Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, Article 36

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and state: 'I wish to remain silent.'
Do not carry false documents.
Do not sign anything without a lawyer.
Memorize the ActionNYC hotline: (800) 354-0365.
If detained, ask to call your attorney immediately.

rights.description: You may decline to answer questions from law enforcement at any time.
Officers need a warrant, probable cause, or your consent to conduct a search.
You have the right to an attorney. In New York, the right to counsel attaches when formal proceedings begin or when an attorney enters the matter.
You may record police in public. NY is a one-party consent state.
NYPD officers must provide a business card with their name, rank, and badge number.

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and be respectful.
Keep your hands visible.
Clearly invoke your rights.
Do not physically resist.
Document everything afterward.

TX.name: Texas
state_specific_notes: Texas is a one-party consent state for recordings (TX Penal Code Section 16.02). You may record your interactions with police.
Texas has a 'Failure to Identify' law (TX Penal Code Section 38.02) that requires you to identify yourself when lawfully arrested or detained.
Texas has broad 'Castle Doctrine' protections for homeowners (TX Penal Code Section 9.31-9.32).
Texas does not have sanctuary city protections; SB 4 (2017) requires local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
Open carry of handguns without a permit is legal in Texas for adults 21+ under HB 1927 (2021).

rights.description: Texas law requires you to provide your name, date of birth, and address when lawfully detained. You must show your driver's license during a traffic stop.
rights.source: TX Penal Code Section 38.02; TX Transportation Code Section 521.025

rights.right: Right to Remain Silent Beyond Identification
rights.description: After providing identification, you have the right to remain silent. You do not have to answer questions about where you are going or coming from.
rights.source: 5th Amendment; TX Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 38.22

rights.description: You do not have to consent to a vehicle search. Without consent, officers need probable cause or a warrant.
rights.source: 4th Amendment; TX Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 18.01

rights.description: Texas is a one-party consent state. You may freely record your traffic stop.
If arrested, you have the right to an attorney. Texas law requires magistrate warnings within 48 hours of arrest.
rights.source: 6th Amendment; TX Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 15.17

de_escalation_tips: Keep both hands on the steering wheel.
If you have a firearm, inform the officer immediately.
Do not exit the vehicle unless asked.
Provide ID when requested -- it is required by Texas law.
Do not argue; contest citations in court.

rights.description: Ask: 'Am I being detained?' If not detained, you may leave. If detained, Texas law requires you to identify yourself.
rights.source: TX Penal Code Section 38.02; Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968)

rights.description: If lawfully detained, you must provide your name, date of birth, and address. Failure to do so is a criminal offense in Texas.

rights.right: Right to Remain Silent Beyond ID
rights.description: Beyond identifying information, you have the right to remain silent.
You may refuse a search of your person unless the officer has reasonable suspicion you are armed.
You may record police interactions in public spaces.
rights.source: 1st Amendment; Turner v. Driver, 848 F.3d 678 (5th Cir. 2017)

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and keep your hands visible.
Provide identification if lawfully detained -- Texas requires it.
Ask politely: 'Am I free to go?'
Do not physically resist.
Note the time, location, and officer details.

rights.right: Right to Refuse Entry Without a Warrant
rights.description: Texas has strong Castle Doctrine protections. You do not have to let police in without a warrant.
rights.source: 4th Amendment; TX Penal Code Section 9.31; Payton v. New York, 445 U.S. 573 (1980)

rights.description: Ask to see the warrant. Verify it is signed by a judge and lists the correct address.
rights.source: 4th Amendment; TX Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 18.04

rights.description: You do not have to answer questions at your door.
Texas law provides strong protections for residents in their home. However, this does NOT authorize force against police with a valid warrant.
You may request an attorney before answering any questions.

de_escalation_tips: Do not open the door. Talk through the door.
Ask: 'Do you have a warrant signed by a judge?'
If they have a valid warrant, do not resist entry.
Do not threaten officers or brandish weapons.
Call an attorney as soon as possible.

rights.description: You have the right to peacefully protest in public spaces in Texas.
rights.source: 1st Amendment; TX Constitution Art. I, Section 27

rights.description: Texas courts have affirmed the right to record police. The 5th Circuit ruled this is protected by the 1st Amendment.
If detained during a protest, you must provide identification under Texas law.
Beyond identifying yourself, you have the right to remain silent.
Officers may not use excessive force against peaceful protesters.

de_escalation_tips: Protest peacefully and do not block roadways.
Comply with dispersal orders.
If detained, provide identification as required by Texas law.
Keep your hands visible and avoid confrontations.
Have a legal contact number ready.

rights.right: Right to Remain Silent About Immigration Status
rights.description: You are not required to answer questions about your immigration status, even in Texas.
If lawfully detained, Texas law requires you to provide your name, date of birth, and address. This does not include immigration status.
You have the right to an attorney before answering questions or signing documents related to immigration.
You generally have the right to appear before an immigration judge before deportation.
Foreign nationals have the right to contact their consulate if detained.
rights.source: Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, Article 36

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and do not run.
State: 'I wish to remain silent.'
Provide identifying information if lawfully detained.
Do not provide false information -- it is a crime in Texas.
Do not sign anything without consulting an attorney.

rights.description: Texas requires identification when lawfully detained. Beyond that, you may remain silent.
Officers need a warrant, probable cause, or your consent to search.
rights.source: 4th Amendment; TX Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 18.01

rights.description: You have the right to an attorney if arrested.
rights.source: 6th Amendment; TX Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 1.05

rights.description: You may record police in public. Texas courts have affirmed this right.
rights.source: 1st Amendment; Turner v. Driver, 848 F.3d 678 (5th Cir. 2017)

rights.description: You may file a complaint against an officer with their department's internal affairs division.

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and be respectful.
Provide ID when lawfully required.
Keep your hands visible.
Invoke your rights clearly.
Document the encounter afterward.

FL.name: Florida
state_specific_notes: Florida is a two-party consent state for recording oral communications (FL Statute Section 934.03). However, recording police in public where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy is generally protected.
Florida has a 'Stop and Frisk' law (FL Statute Section 901.151) allowing officers to temporarily detain persons suspected of crime.
Florida has a 'Stand Your Ground' law (FL Statute Section 776.012-776.013) but this does NOT apply to encounters with law enforcement.
Florida requires you to provide identification only when lawfully detained and the officer has reasonable suspicion.
Florida has no statewide sanctuary city policy; SB 168 (2019) requires local cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

rights.description: Provide your license, registration, and insurance. Beyond that, you have the right to remain silent.
rights.source: 5th Amendment; FL Constitution Art. I, Section 9

rights.description: You do not have to consent to a vehicle search. State clearly: 'I do not consent to a search.'
rights.source: 4th Amendment; FL Constitution Art. I, Section 12

rights.description: You may visually record a traffic stop. Florida is a two-party consent state for audio of private conversations, but interactions with police in public are not considered private.
rights.source: 1st Amendment; FL Statute Section 934.03; Smith v. City of Cumming, 212 F.3d 1332 (11th Cir. 2000)

rights.right: Right to Know the Reason for the Stop
rights.description: You may ask why you were pulled over. Officers need at least reasonable suspicion of a violation.
If arrested, invoke your right to an attorney. Florida has public defender services in every judicial circuit.
rights.source: 6th Amendment; FL Constitution Art. I, Section 16

de_escalation_tips: Pull over safely and turn on your hazard lights.
Keep your hands on the steering wheel.
Turn on interior lights at night.
Tell the officer before reaching for anything.
Do not argue -- handle disputes in court.

rights.right: Right to Ask if You Are Detained
rights.description: Ask: 'Am I being detained or am I free to go?' Officers need reasonable suspicion under Florida's Stop and Frisk law to detain you.
rights.source: FL Statute Section 901.151; Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968)

rights.description: Florida does not have a mandatory stop-and-identify statute for pedestrians. You may decline to answer questions.
rights.source: 5th Amendment; FL Constitution Art. I, Section 9

rights.description: You may refuse a search of your person. Officers may conduct a limited pat-down only if they reasonably suspect you are armed.
You may record police interactions in public.
rights.source: 1st Amendment; Smith v. City of Cumming, 212 F.3d 1332 (11th Cir. 2000)

rights.right: Right to Walk Away if Not Detained
rights.description: If you are not being detained, you have every right to calmly walk away.

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and keep your hands visible.
Politely ask: 'Am I free to go?'
If detained, remain composed and invoke your rights.
Do not run or physically resist.
Make mental notes of the officer's badge number and appearance.

rights.right: Right to Refuse Entry Without a Warrant
rights.description: You are not required to open your door or allow police into your home without a valid judicial warrant.
rights.source: 4th Amendment; FL Constitution Art. I, Section 12; Payton v. New York, 445 U.S. 573 (1980)

rights.description: Ask to see the warrant through a window or have it slid under the door. Check that it is signed by a judge and has the correct address.
rights.source: 4th Amendment; FL Rule of Criminal Procedure 3.121

rights.description: You do not have to speak with officers at your door.
You may request an attorney before answering any questions.
If officers enter with a valid warrant, you may observe the search and ask for an inventory of items seized.

de_escalation_tips: Do not open the door. Speak through it.
Ask: 'Do you have a warrant signed by a judge?'
If they have a valid warrant, do not physically resist.
Call a lawyer immediately.
Ask for a receipt for any items taken.

rights.description: You have the right to peacefully protest in public areas in Florida.
rights.source: 1st Amendment; FL Constitution Art. I, Section 5

rights.description: You may record police and protest activity in public spaces.
rights.source: 1st Amendment; Smith v. City of Cumming, 212 F.3d 1332 (11th Cir. 2000)

rights.description: Officers should give a clear dispersal order before making arrests for unlawful assembly.

rights.right: Right to Remain Silent if Detained
rights.description: If detained during a protest, you have the right to remain silent and request an attorney.
Florida's HB 1 increased penalties for protest-related offenses including blocking roads and damaging property. Peaceful protest remains protected.

de_escalation_tips: Protest peacefully and stay on sidewalks.
Do not block roadways -- Florida has enhanced penalties for this.
Follow dispersal orders promptly.
Have a legal support number written down.
Do not engage in property destruction -- penalties are severe under HB 1.

rights.right: Right to Remain Silent About Immigration Status
rights.description: You are not required to answer questions about where you were born or your immigration status.
You have the right to consult with an attorney before answering immigration-related questions or signing documents.

rights.right: Right to Refuse to Sign Documents
rights.description: Do not sign voluntary departure or other immigration documents without speaking to a lawyer.
In most cases, you have the right to a hearing before an immigration judge.
rights.source: INA Section 240; Zadvydas v. Davis, 533 U.S. 678 (2001)

rights.description: Foreign nationals may contact their country's consulate if detained.
rights.source: Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, Article 36

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and do not flee.
Say: 'I am exercising my right to remain silent.'
Do not carry false documents.
Do not sign anything without a lawyer.
Know the Florida Immigrant Coalition hotline number.

rights.description: You may decline to answer questions from law enforcement under the 5th Amendment and the Florida Constitution.
rights.source: 5th Amendment; FL Constitution Art. I, Section 9

rights.description: Florida's constitution provides search and seizure protections similar to the 4th Amendment.
rights.source: 4th Amendment; FL Constitution Art. I, Section 12

rights.description: You have the right to an attorney at all critical stages of criminal proceedings.
rights.source: 6th Amendment; FL Constitution Art. I, Section 16

rights.description: You may record police performing public duties in public spaces.
rights.source: 1st Amendment; Smith v. City of Cumming, 212 F.3d 1332 (11th Cir. 2000)

rights.description: You may file a complaint against an officer with their agency's internal affairs or the Florida Department of Law Enforcement.

de_escalation_tips: Stay calm and be respectful.
Keep your hands visible.
Invoke your rights calmly.
Do not physically resist.
Document the encounter afterward with notes and any recordings.
